Paragraph Text: You might be able to make a new immigration application based on human rights.This might be because of the connections you have in the UK, or because of your particular circumstances. If your application is not based on protection grounds, you can submit this using an online form and submitting your evidence to the Home Office.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Most people in the community care about the people around them, and they want their community to feel safe and fair.There are however some individuals and groups that support far-right extremists, or support anti-migrant and racist ideas. These people target and intimidate those who look different to them or who have different beliefs to them. If you are worried about your safety, you can read and share ourGeneral Safety advicewhich explains lots of practical ways to stay safe, get support and look out for each other. There are different steps you can take, and processes to follow in different situations: If you feel unsafe in asylum accommodation • Tell migrant help, explain your concern, ask for a safe place to stay • If you have been threatened or attacked, call the police • Contact a trusted person, consider staying with a friend • Find a local support organisation and explain what is happening If you have been discriminated against in a service setting (e.g. GP, job centre) • Ask to speak to a different member of staff or a manager • Ask for another appointment or a specific time to talk about what happened. You can take a trusted person with you for support. • Write down what happened, how it affected you and what you want to happen. You can ask a trusted person to help you do this. • Ask what the complaint process is, or check their website to find out. You can make a formal complaint if you don’t feel comfortable speaking to someone directly or if you feel it is important to do this. A formal complaint sometimes means that the service must respond and take action, and sometimes it will be noted on the service’s public record that a complaint has been made (the details of the complaint should not be shared).A complaint might not lead to the outcome that you want, or any action at all, but it can be an important way of being heard and stopping further incidents from happening. If you have been attacked or threatened in public • Seek a safe space. This might be in a cafe, a place of worship or a shop. • Try to stay calm and keep space from the attacker • Call the police to report an incident or threat or if you are in danger • Contact a trusted person to talk about what happened or to have some company • Remember that it is not your fault and it is not OK

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Having information and documents as evidence to prove your situation can be really important when you make an immigration or asylum application. Decisions on cases can be very slow, but there are also some new processes with shorter deadlines, for example forasylum appeals.Where possible, having evidence ready early in a case can be helpful for your case. Keeping your documents organised can be a helpful step to take to prepare yourself. Having copies of your documents that you can access easily will help you be ready if you need to explain your situation or submit evidence quickly. There are a few things you can do to gather and organise your documents: • Check you have copies of important Home Office documents.This can include:Interview recordsHome Office decision lettersReporting and bail documents • Interview records • Home Office decision letters • Reporting and bail documents • Check you have copies of any court documents like Judge’s decisions • Check you have copies of any evidence you submitted and proof it was submitted.This can include:Your witness statementImportant documentsReports and articles (you might want to save a link if they are online but also download or print the page) • Your witness statement • Important documents • Reports and articles (you might want to save a link if they are online but also download or print the page) If you have lost some of your documents, there are different ways you can get copies: • Make a subject access request to the Home Office • If a lawyer helped with your case, ask them for your file. Find out more about working with lawyershere • Ask for copies of your court documents:Login to HMCTS to find a copyEmail the court:contactia@justice.gov.uk • Login to HMCTS to find a copy • Email the court:contactia@justice.gov.uk If you have been in the UK for a long time, then you might want to find evidence to show that you have been living here. This can include lots of different types of evidence. We have listed some of themabove. You might be able to ask someone you know and trust to write you letters, or you might need to make a more formal request by writing a letter or email to services you have used, places you have worked or volunteered, or anywhere else you might have been present. Your letter might look something like this: [Addressed to the person or service] RE: Letter of support for [Your name and date of birth] Dear Sir or Madam I am writing to request a letter from you regarding my involvement with your service/ attendance at your service. The letter is required as evidence of my presence in the UK as part of an immigration application.I kindly request that you provide me with a short letter confirming the following details: • Your name and position • How you know me or know of me • The dates during which I had contact with your service • The nature of my contact Thank you kindly for your assistance. Yours Sincerely, Sometimes, a service might tell you that they no longer hold your information and cannot provide this. Normally this happens because of data protection, which is a system designed to stop your information being stored or shared when it is not necessary.Many services will delete your information and documents if you have not contacted them for a certain period of time. This can make it difficult to get evidence to prove that you were in the UK a long time ago. You might want to consider keeping multiple copies of your documents.This could mean having your documents printed and stored in a folder in a safe place, like in your home or with a service you trust. You could also have a digital copy of your documents saved in your emails, or an online storage system.If there is someone you trust who could keep a copy of your documents for you in a file, or online, then this could also help you access them in a crisis.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you are living somewhere that is not safe, suitable or accessible, you might want to ask for a different type of support. A lot of people experience issues with the accommodation provided through asylum support. Houses are often in poor condition and need repairs. This can make it uncomfortable to live in a property, and sometimes unsafe.It is important to report any issues to the Home Office to ask them to make the property safe and secure. Often, when you first ask for asylum support, you will be given a room in a hotel. Sometimes you will be told to share a room with someone else. This is called emergency accommodation and should only be for a short time.In reality, many people have to live in hotels for a long time, which can mean not being able to cook your own meals, and having to share space with unfamiliar people.This can be hard, particularly if you have experienced trauma, or abuse. Sometimes, if you are living in a hotel, you will be told that you won’t be given money to support yourself, but will be given food at the hotel. The food can be different to what you are used to or would like to eat, and there are often no cooking facilities for you to cook for yourself. If you or your child have special dietary requirements, you can explain this and make a request for different arrangements but this might not be accepted if the Home Office decides the food is suitable. If you are given asylum support, the Home Office can decide to move you to a different place at any time. You won’t have a choice about where you will live.You could be moved somewhere far away, or somewhere that is very remote (this means it is not close to a town or services). This can also happen with very little notice. It can be difficult to move if you have been in an area for a long time, for example if you have made connections in the community, found a lawyer nearby, are receiving medical treatment or have children in school.You can explain to the Home Office that you do not want to move, and explain why you need to stay in your area. The Home Office might consider this information and offer you a different property, or they might refuse and tell you that you have to move anyway. For any accommodation issues or requests, it is important to try and provide as much information and evidence as possible. If you refuse to go to the accommodation offered to you, then the Home Office can record this as ‘failure to travel’. Sometimes this happens by accident, for example if you didn’t know you were going to be moved, or because the person who comes to collect you goes to the wrong address. If you are told that you failed to travel, then it is important to explain why, so that you can request to be taken to the accommodation again or to ask for a different option. If your explanation is not accepted then you might need to apply again for support. Sometimes, your circumstances could change while you are in asylum support, for example if you have a child, or separate from a partner. You might be sharing a room, or a property, and feel uncomfortable or unsafe because of other residents. If you need different accommodation because your accommodation is not suitable or accessible, you don’t feel safe, or you want to live separately from someone else then you can explain this and ask to be moved. If you are in danger, and need to move urgently, then you should report this as soon as possible. You can talk to a housing officer, or a trusted person who can support you to do this. You might be able to access asafe housein some situations. In an emergency, call 999. There has been an increase of attacks on asylum support housing. If you think that your home is being targeted, or you have been threatened, then you can report this to the police, and to the Home Office. If there is a trusted person that you can contact in your area, then they could also help you to seek safety and report what is happening.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: Asking to return to the country you are from
Paragraph Text: There is a process called ‘voluntary return’ which you can apply to if you want to return to the country you are from. This is different to being removed or deported from the UK because it is not considered a forced removal. The Home Office might share information about voluntary return to you if you receive a refusal letter.Although this process is voluntary, sometimes it is explained in a way that can make you feel pressured to make an application for return, even if you don’t want to.If you feel like you are being pressured to ask for voluntary return, you can say that you don’t want to discuss this. Applying for voluntary return means that you can ask for asylum support while you wait to be returned to your country. It might feel like this is your only option if you have nowhere to live and no money to support yourself, and you don’t feel able to make a new immigration or asylum application yet.If your case has been refused, and you have been told that your support will stop, it can be really confusing and difficult to know what to do next. Asking for voluntary return can impact your immigration status, so it is important to consider whether you really want to be returned to the country you are from. If you ask for voluntary return and then change your mind, then you can withdraw your application, but this could affect future applications. For example, if you ask for voluntary return, then make a fresh claim for asylum, then the Home Office could say that you would be safe in the country you are from because you asked to return there. If this happens to you then you can explain why you made the request and what has changed. Sometimes, you might decide that you want to return to the country you are from. This could be because your circumstances have changed, the situation in your country has improved or because you don’t want to live in the UK. If you apply for voluntary return, you can also request financial support from the Home Office. This can help you support yourself when you arrive in your home country.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Asylum support is provided by the Home Office. There are different types of asylum support which are usually named after the section of the law where they are explained. The main types are called ‘Section 98’, ‘Section 95’, ‘section 4’ and ‘schedule 10’. The support you can access will depend on the stage of your case, and your individual circumstances. You can apply for asylum support if: • You have made a first claim for asylum, have not received a final decision and have nowhere to live or no money to support yourself; • You have claimed asylum and received a refusal decision, and you have no more appeal rightsand:You have asked for help from the Home Office to return to the country you are from;orYou are not able to leave the UK because of a medical condition (a doctor must confirm in writing that you are not able to travel on a plane);orThere is no safe way to travel to the country you are from;orYou have permission to request a judicial review about your asylum claim;orSupport is needed to protect your human rights – this includes if you have made further submissions to the Home Office. • You have asked for help from the Home Office to return to the country you are from;or • You are not able to leave the UK because of a medical condition (a doctor must confirm in writing that you are not able to travel on a plane);or • There is no safe way to travel to the country you are from;or • You have permission to request a judicial review about your asylum claim;or • Support is needed to protect your human rights – this includes if you have made further submissions to the Home Office. • You are on immigration bail, you have been told that you need to stay in a specific address and you have nowhere to live.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: There are lots of charity and community organisations providing support to different groups of people. This could include housing, financial support, support and advice services, clothes and food, or something else.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: There are lots of charities in the UK, providing different types of support. This could include: • Helping you access and understand services • Providing advice and support • Help with living costs or transport costs • English lessons • Activities and community events for wellbeing You can check if there are any support services in your local area by searching online. You can also contact bigger, national organisations to ask for help to access support. Some organisations only support specific groups of people. Support can include connecting you with other people in your community, or helping you understand and navigate different situations. It could also be help with money, food or clothes. If you are pregnant, you might be able to get support to understand your maternity rights, or help you when you give birth. You may also be able to get help with money or for clothes and items for your baby. If you identify as LGBTQI, there are lots of different organisations that can support you by sharing information and connecting you with a community. If you have a disability, you might be entitled to extra support.Sometimes professionals are misinformed about who is entitled to what, and the legal duties of a particular service. This can often be a barrier for adults with care needs, and for people seeking asylum who have a disability. There are lots of resources online that explain rights and entitlements, as well as some organisations providing support and advocacy. If you have been diagnosed with a mental health condition, or you are feeling very low or anxious, you might be able to access therapy or counselling.If you think you are having a mental health crisis and you are at risk you can call 999 or go to A&E.There also might be a community support group near you where you can go and meet other people or take part in activities. If you are struggling, your GP can also help you understand any possible treatment options, or refer you to a specialist if needed.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: There are different situations where your asylum support can be stopped. This is called a discontinuation.If the Home Office plans to stop giving you asylum support, then they should send you a letter explaining this.You support might be stopped if: • You receive a decision on your asylum claim • The Home Office thinks you are not living in the accommodation • The Home Office thinks you are not destitute – this can include if they believe you have a bank account or are working • Your asylum claim is withdrawn – this can happen if you miss a reporting event, or an interview, or if you breach bail conditions, for example by working without permission If you receive a discontinuation letter, try to read through this and understand why your support is being stopped. If your claim has been withdrawn then you will need to take action to restart your claim.You might be able to challenge a discontinuation decision by explaining things or providing evidence. If you have received a decision on your asylum claim, then your options will depend on whether your claim is refused or accepted. If you are granted protection status or leave to remain, then you will have a limited time (currently 42 days) to find another place to stay. You can check whether you can access housing through the local authority and follow the local application process. You might be able to find support to do this through an organisation supporting migrant communities in your area. If your asylum claim is refused, you will need to check whether you have a right of appeal against the decision. If you do, then the appeal deadline is 14 days from the date of the decision.It is important that you lodge an appeal in time to make sure that your support continues. If you miss the appeal deadline, then you can still lodge an appeal and ask for asylum support again but this can be more complicated.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Immigration control can make it harder for migrant communities to access services but there are also often other barriers. Some of these are built into systems and institutions themselves, while others come from racism, discrimination and hostility in wider society. This does not mean that everyone in a community is hostile or racist. But loud anti-migrant voices, parts of the mainstream media, organised far-right groups and discriminatory systems can all shape how safe or welcome people feel, and how they are treated when trying to access support or services. This could include: • Language and communication barriers– if you don’t speak English, or find it hard to understand or communicate • Being made to feel unwelcome or discriminated against– this means being treated differently because of your identity or circumstances. It could be someone refusing to help you, or provide a certain service to you, by ignoring you, or through offensive words or actions • Lack of respect for religious or cultural requirements– this could mean being refused a chaperone or female doctor, or not being allowed an appropriate place to pray • Lack of professional knowledge– when services don’t understand your rights and entitlements, they can refuse to support you or make accessing support confusing and intimidating • Feeling scared– of being asked to pay, of being reported to the Home Office, of being targeted These barriers can make accessing services feel intimidating. If possible, going with someone you trust to appointments and making connections in your community can help you feel safer. If someone treats you differently because of your race, religion, gender, sexuality or a disability, they could be committing a criminal offence.It can feel overwhelming and scary to say something, but if you feel able to, then you can report this as a hate crime to the police. If you feel threatened or targeted in a service, or if things just don’t feel right, try to find a space where you feel safe, or contact someone you trust to explain what is happening. You can think about how you feel and what you want to do next. This could be reporting an incident, making a complaint, or finding a different service to use. Sometimes, abuse and violence can happen when you are in a public space, or in your accommodation. Verbal abuse, threats, harassment and violent attacks can all be criminal offences, and are not acceptable in any situation. If you are threatened directly, or repeatedly, then you can report this to the police, and if you think you are at immediate risk of harm then call 999.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you are living in an abusive situation, then you might not have control of your own activities or finances. You might feel like you need to keep your job because someone is threatening you by controlling your income, or because you want to be able to leave the situation and support yourself independently. When this is done by a family member, it is called domestic abuse. There are support options available if you are in this situation, and your safety is the most important thing. We explain what you might be able to do if you are in this situation in our Key Guide for migrants affected by domestic abuse.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you are in the UK without leave to remain, then you are at higher risk of being targeted by Home Office enforcement because of your immigration status. Enforcement can happen in different situations and forms, including through immigration visits, checks and raids. This could be in a public space or on public transport, or in a targeted raid in a home, or a workplace. If a visit or raid happens in a place where you are living, or working, then you could be questioned, and detained, but there are some rules about when and how this can happen.Immigration officers cannot just stop you and question you if they have no permission or clear reason to do so.We explain more about immigration enforcement and your rights in our Immigration Enforcement Key Guide. If you have submitted an application to remain in the UK, then you should not be removed while this is being considered.This does not mean that you cannot be questioned or detained and you could still face criminal charges if you are breaking the law. This can include doing things you don’t have permission to do, for example working when you don’t have the right to work. Any criminal charge can affect your immigration or asylum case and be used as a reason to remove you from the UK, so it is important to understand and consider this.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: When people have very limited choices about how to get money, food, housing or other things they need, this can make them more vulnerable to unsafe or unfair situations.Someone else may treat you badly, pressure you to do things you do not want to do, take advantage of your situation, or control where you go and what you do. If this is happening to you, then you might be experiencing exploitation.Exploitation happens when a person who is in a position of power abuses their power to control another person for their own benefit,for example to make money. Being exploited is not your fault, even if you agreed to the situation at first or felt you had no other option. Exploitation is not always visible or obvious. It can happen in many different relationships, work or living situations .It happens when someone makes you do something you don’t want to do, controls your activities or movement, or refuses to give you something that was agreed. This could include: • Taking or keeping your passport, ID, bank card or phone • Threatening to report you to the Home Office, police or another authority • Stopping you from leaving, seeing other people or contacting friends and family • Pressuring or forcing you to do work or other things you did not agree to • Changing your pay, hours or conditions after you have already started • Making you pay unfair or unexpected charges for accommodation, transport, food or work • Threatening to make you homeless if you do not do what they say • Controlling your money or taking money from your account • Pressuring or forcing you into sexual activity • Making you commit crimes or do things that could get you into trouble • Making you work in unsafe conditions If you do not have leave to remain, or if your immigration status is temporary or depends on your job, you may feel that you cannot leave a situation where you are being exploited. Your immigration status may also make it feel harder or less safe to report what is happening or ask for help. The immigration system can itself feel unsafe and uncertain. Being exploited is not your fault.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: A food bank is a place where you can go and access free food if you have a low income or are experiencing destitution.There is a local food bank in most areas in the UK. Sometimes, food banks will ask you to bring proof of your circumstances. This might be a letter showing that you are receiving asylum support, a bank statement or a letter from a support service who have told you to go to the food bank. There are lots of local organisations that can also help you to get clothes that are appropriate for the weather, like a coat or shoes.If you have children then you might also be able to get support to find free school uniforms, from a charity, from a school or from the local authority.You can check for local services online by searching for ‘free clothes’ and your area.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If your asylum claim was refused and you have no more appeal rights, you might be able to submit more information or evidence by making further submissions.You can do this at any point in your case, even if it has been a long time since you came to the UK or received a refusal. There are some general principles to understand if you are thinking about making further submissions which we explain in the Fresh claim toolkit page. If you have made further submissions, you can request financial support and housing from the Home Office by applying for asylum support.We explain what this is below, and on our asylum support toolkit page.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: There are some organisations that can help you find a place to stay while you are working on your immigration or asylum case. This could be shared housing that is provided by a charity, or it could be through a hosting arrangement where you live with someone who has offered to share a space in their home. You can try and search for support online by checking the No Accommodation network (NACCOM) member list to see if there is somewhere near you that might be able to help.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: How information is shared by some public services with the Home Office
Paragraph Text: The UK’s hostile environment makes immigration control part of everyday life.Instead of immigration enforcement happening only through reporting, raids, detention or removal, checks on immigration status have been built into areas such as work, housing, healthcare, benefits and other public services. This means people may be asked to prove their immigration status when trying to access things they need.In some situations, services can share information with the Home Office, and the Home Office can confirm things like whether someone has permission to be in the UK, whether they have a right to access a service, or whether there are restrictions on their immigration status. Services that may share information with the Home Office include: • hospitals and healthcare services • local authorities, including children’s and adults’ social services • landlords and employers, where they need to check a person’s right to rent or work • Jobcentres, when checking entitlement to benefits or other support These systems can make people feel watched, unsure about their rights, or scared to ask for help. They can also create barriers for people who do have a right to access a service. But knowing that information sharing can happen does not mean that people should avoid services they need. In many situations, services can only ask for or share certain information for particular reasons. Where possible, you can ask why information is being requested, whether it will be shared with the Home Office, and what information is actually needed. You can also take someone you trust with you, ask for an interpreter if you need one, and keep a record of what you were asked for and what happened. If you need urgent medical attention or you are in danger, your safety and wellbeing comes first. Do not avoid emergency help because you are worried about information sharing. The police can share your details with Immigration Enforcement. In some situations, police officers also have powers to arrest someone under immigration law. They cannot stop, question or arrest someone just because of assumptions about their nationality, ethnicity or immigration status. Community organisations and specialist services may also be able to help you understand your rights, challenge unfair treatment and navigate these systems more safely.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: How your immigration status affects your rights in the UK
Paragraph Text: To understand what your rights are, you need to understand what your immigration status is.Your immigration status means the legal permission you have (or do not have) to be in the UK. If you are in the UK with indefinite leave to remain, settled status or as a British Citizen, then there are no restrictions on your right to access most types of support, but you may need to prove other circumstances. If you are in the UK on a temporary visa, or with leave to remain (a type of permission to be in the UK) then you can check whether there are any conditions attached to your immigration status. If you have claimed asylum and are waiting for a decision, then you will have access to specifictypes of support. If you don’t have any type of visa, your leave to remain has expired, or you have never applied for permission to be in the UK, then you have no leave to remain.People in this situation might hear the terms ‘overstayer’ or ‘undocumented migrant’ or be told they have no immigration status. The conditions attached to different types of immigration status mean that there are certain people who are more likely to be at risk of destitution. This can include: • people who have claimed asylum (especially when they have been refused). • people with no recourse to public funds (this means that you cannot access certain kinds of financial help or housing support from the government or your local council. It is often shortened to NRPF) • people who are in the UK without leave to remain. There are many reasons why someone may be living in the UK without current permission. This can include difficulties caused by the immigration system or things that have happened in someone’s life. Your rights can change at different stages of your case.You might be able to access different support after making an application, or getting a new decision, but you might also lose access to support. Sometimes, you may have had the right to do certain things in the past, for example if you came to the UK on a visa as a student or worker, and then claimed asylum. You may still have access to a job, benefits, a home, a car or a bank account, or be receiving treatment for a medical condition. However, being able to continue accessing somethingdoes not mean that you are legally entitled to this.  This could cause you to face issues later on.For example: • Being told you have a debt to repay e.g. for medical treatment, or for benefits paid to you by mistake • The Home Office deciding to stop your visa • Facing criminal charges e.g. if you are found driving or working without the right to do so It can be difficult to understand whether you are allowed to do something.If you are unsure, check your Home Office documents first. You might find this information in recent decision letters, or immigration bail documents. If it is still unclear, you can ask a trusted person to help you understand your documents or try and get legal advice from a lawyer. If you do not have copies of the documents you need, you can ask the Home Office for them. This is called making aSubject Access Request (SAR).

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: If you are living in the UK without leave to remain
Paragraph Text: This section is about people who are living in the UK without leave to remain and who are not waiting for a decision on an asylum claim. Many people live in the UK without leave to remain.This means they don’t have permission to live in the UK. This might be because their application was refused, because they have stayed past the expiry date of their visa or because they have never made an application to stay in the UK. You might be told you can stay in the UK but you are on “immigration bail”. This means that you can live in the UK but with specific conditions, and that you could be detained by the Home Office. This usually means having to live at a specific address, and report to the Home Office, and sometimes harsher conditions like electronic tagging. If you do not have leave to remain, you will also have no recourse to public funds. You are  not allowed to work, rent accommodation, study, drive, or even open a bank account. You can also be stopped from accessing certain healthcare services, and can be charged for medical treatment. If you require emergency medical treatment, this should be provided but you can be charged afterwards. These conditions can make it very difficult for you to afford your basic needs and keep yourself safe and healthy. If you have no leave to remain, and no application waiting, it is important that you also understand your immigration options so that you have enough information to make decisions about your future. If you are in this situation, you are at greater risk of being detained and removed from the UK. There are still things you can do to take actions to prepare and protect yourself. As communities, we can also take collective action by providing legal support to build solidarity and protect each other. You might want to consider whether there is an asylum or immigration application you could make. If you are granted leave to remain, then you will be able to access more types of support, and if you make further submissions, then you will be able to ask for asylum support. We explain the different types of support more later on the page. Immigration law and Home Office rules are very complicated and change often.You are not expected to understand everything on your own.Even lawyers and judges have said that immigration law can be very difficult to understand and keep up with. We know that reading this information can feel overwhelming, especially if you are dealing with a lot at the same time.You are not alone, and needing help does not mean you have done anything wrong.You can take things one step at a time and ask someone you trust to help you. The Right to Remain Toolkit contains lots of information about the immigration and asylum system, and preparing different types of applications. You can read through this in your own language, or with a trusted person who can help you think about useful steps you could take.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: If you can’t afford to pay for an application
Paragraph Text: If you want to make an immigration application, but you cannot afford the fees, you may be able to request a fee waiver so that you can make your application without paying.To do this, you will need to provide evidence to show that: • You can’t afford your housing or living costs • You are experiencing destitution • You have a low income and paying fees could impact a child’s wellbeing

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you have claimed asylum, then you can normally ask the Home Office to give you somewhere to live and money to support yourself while you wait for a decision. This is called ‘asylum support’. The support you can get depends on your situation and what is happening with your case. We know from our community thatasylum support is often not enough.Some people struggle to afford basic items with the money they are given or have to rely on support from charities, friends, family, people in the community. This means thatmany people who receive asylum support may still be facing destitution. If you make an application for asylum support, the Home Office will first check your financial circumstances.This means they will ask questions about whether you have any income or savings, and why you need asylum support. They can also check with the banks whether you have any accounts, and ask you for bank statements if you do.If you ask for support later in your claim, you might be asked to explain how you have been supporting yourself so far, and where you have been staying. If your asylum claim is refused, you might have a right of appeal.You can continue to receive asylum support until you have no more appeal rights(we explain this morehere). At this stage, you will lose your right to asylum support. You might be able to apply for asylum support again if you make further submissions, or if you ask the Home Office to return you to your country. Some people might be able to keep getting asylum support, even if they have no more appeal rights.  For example, support can continue if your household includes a dependent child under 18. Other people may be able to get a different type of support, calledSection 4 support, if they are destitute and meet certain conditions. This can include some situations where a health problem means they cannot leave the UK There are also circumstances where you may need to get extra support, such as extra payments or accommodation that meets particular needs.This might include: • If you are pregnant • If you have a baby or child aged 3 or under. • If you need to travel a long distance for medical treatment • If you have a health condition that causes extra essential costs e.g. if you need a special diet. • If you have a disability or health condition and need specific accommodation or equipment e.g. because of mobility or other medical needs • If your accommodation is not safe for you or does not meet your important health or support needs. E.g. this could be risk from domestic abuse or harassment. We explain this further below, and you can read more about asylum support below and on our Asylum Support toolkit pagehere.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: If you have ‘no recourse to public funds’
Paragraph Text: Public funds are certain types of financial help and housing support that are listed in immigration law. You will also hear them called ‘benefits’. Benefits are financial support provided by the government which can include money, vouchers, discounted bills and housing.Lots of benefits are public funds, but some are not. Check which benefits are public fundshere. If you have leave to remain in the UK, you might have a condition called ‘no recourse to public funds’. You should be able to check this on your evisa, and you can also check the decision letter for when your application was granted.If you have ‘no recourse to public funds’ (NRPF) then you will not be allowed to claim any public funds. NRPF is part of the hostile environment – a system of rules designed to make life more difficult for migrants who are in the UK without permission or with temporary status. The government says that restricting rights for certain migrants is necessary for immigration enforcement so that people do not enter the UK without permission, or stay in the UK without permission. They also say that these restrictions protect ‘taxpayer money’. In reality, these restrictions often leave people without enough money, housing or other support and increase risk of destitution. You might have a NRPF restriction if you are in the UK with leave to remain as: For many people, this condition means that they are trying to survive on a low wage, or with no income and cannot apply for support from the government to help cover their living costs. This can be difficult if your circumstances change without warning. For example if a relationship breaks down, if you lose your job, or if you become responsible for caring for a child or family member. Some people will be able to request access to public funds if they are not able to afford their basic living costs, if they are responsible for a child, or if they have lost or could lose their housing. This is done by making an application called ‘change of conditions’.  Making this request can impact your immigration status, so it’s important to understand this before applying.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Immigration enforcement means all of the ways that the Home Office controls immigration.This can be tracking and controlling where someone lives or can go, telling someone to report, or through detention and removal. Enforcement also happens through the hostile environment, which is a system that restricts people’s rights based on their immigration status by pushing immigration checks into everyday life.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: A local authority means the local government in the area where you live.The local authorities are legally responsible for supporting certain people.There are two main reasons why this support could be given: • a child (under 18) is in need of additional support because they are at risk or there is no responsible adult to care for them • An adult is assessed as having ‘eligible care needs’ and requires support to ensure their wellbeing and safety Before the local authority can provide support, they will complete an assessment. This can take a long time and be complicated. Sometimes, assessments can be incorrect or missing information, and support can be refused.If the local authority refuses to support you, you might be able to challenge this decision.You can try to provide more information or evidence, or you can look for a community care solicitor to help you.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: You will usually need to make a new application to be granted leave to remain. Different applications could also give you access to different types of support.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Sometimes, exploitation can be so severe that it becomes modern slavery or human trafficking under the law. Modern slaveryincludes situations where someone is forced, threatened, deceived or controlled in order to exploit them. This might include being forced to work, being sexually exploited, being made to commit crimes, or being prevented from leaving an exploitative situation. You do not have to be completely controlled by another person for your experience to be considered modern slavery. Traffickingis a type of modern slavery. It involves someone being recruited, moved, transferred, housed or received so that they can be exploited. This could involve labour exploitation, sexual exploitation, criminal exploitation or other types of exploitation. There is a special system for identifying and supporting people who may have experienced modern slavery or trafficking. This is called the National Referral Mechanism (NRM).Depending on your circumstances and the stage of the process, support can include accommodation, financial support and help to access healthcare and other services. Adults must agree before they are referred into the NRM, and the referral must usually be made by an organisation that is allowed to make referrals, called a first responder organisation. You can ask for help even if the exploitation happened a long time ago, and you do not need to be certain that what happened to you was modern slavery before asking for support. If you think you may be experiencing modern slavery or trafficking now, you can speak to someone you trust or a specialist organisation about your options. If you are in immediate danger, you can call 999.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you think you might have experiencedmodern slavery or trafficking, you can ask to be given a safe place to stay and money to support yourself while you think about your next steps. This is normally arranged through the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), which is a government process for identifying and supporting people in this situation. Referrals to the NRM are usually made through theSalvation Armyor by a specific person, but you can also call and report this yourself.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Strict immigration rules mean that often, people spend a long time in the UK before they can make an application. You might choose to stay in the UK if you know that the country you are from is unsafe or unstable, and this has not been accepted by the Home Office or courts. If you plan on making an application based on the time you have spent in the UK, and the connections you have to the UK, then you will need to be able to provide evidence.Gathering evidence early and keeping copies of your documents can be really helpful for when you make an application. Data protection law means that services can delete your information after a certain period of time. This can make it more difficult to get information later on. If you can, keep copies of all your documents by saving them as digital files. You might also want to give physical copies of your documents to someone you trust who can keep these somewhere safe for you. Things that could be useful for proving time spent in the UK might include: • Letters or emails confirming paid or voluntary work, payslips, tax returns, national insurance records • Home Office documents • Medical letters and records • Bank statements • Certificates from education or training • Bills and rent agreements • Membership documents or ID

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you have leave to remain, and there is no NRPF condition, then you can apply for benefits if you need help with your living costs or accommodation. You will need to meet the rules for each specific type of support. This usually means your income and circumstances will be checked to confirm whether you qualify. You can check what benefits you could get by using online benefit calculators. If you have leave to remain but do not have recourse to public funds, then you might be able to apply specific benefits that are not classed as public funds. You can find a list of thesehere. You also might be able to apply to have the NRPF condition removed. This is done by completing an application called a ‘change of conditions’ using an online form, and giving information about your circumstances.It is important to consider whether this is the best option for you, and whether it might impact your immigration status.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you are in a situation where you feel unsafe because of your identity or because of how you are being treated, then you might be able to get special support and housing.This might mean that you can live in a type of accommodation called a refuge, which is a property that has extra safety measures in place, and support staff available to protect and help the people living there. You might be able to access this support if: • you have been affected by domestic abuse • you may have experienced modern slavery or trafficking (explained above [link in text?]) • you feel unsafe because of your sexuality or gender identity If you think you have experienced or are experiencing domestic abuse, you can seek help to access a refuge. This type of support gives you a safe place to live while you plan your next steps. If you identify as LGBTQI, you might be able to apply to stay in a safe house with other LGBTQI people.  Microrainbow can provide safe housing and social support for people who are waiting for a decision on an asylum claim or a fresh claim.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you have claimed asylum and have been waiting for 12 months or more for a decision from the Home Office, then you might be able to ask for permission to work. If you are given permission to work, you will only be allowed to do certain jobs.If you do a job that is not on the allowed list, you could be told that you are working illegally and you could be told you are committing a crime.Sometimes this can be given as a reason for stopping your asylum support Asylum support is only provided to people who are experiencing destitution.If you start to receive enough income to support yourself through your job, then the Home Office can also say that you are no longer destitute and stop your asylum support. The rules on who can receive asylum support and who can work have changed recently. It is possible that they will change again so it is important to check this or seek legal advice if you plan to ask for permission to work.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: The asylum and immigration systems are not safe. They are designed to be hostile, and the law is complicated. Learning about these systems through our toolkit can help you to understand your situation and your options. Sharing this information in our communities, and taking practical steps to support each other and build solidarity can help us prepare and organise for safer situations.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: Surviving the hostile environment: rights and restrictions
Paragraph Text: If your asylum claim has been refused and you cannot appeal again, or if your visa has ended and you cannot afford an application fee, you no longer meet the immigration rules, or you did not know what to do or could not get legal advice, you may feel unsure about what to do next. You might have been told that the country you are from is safe, and that you can return there, even if you know that you would not be safe. You may have lived in the UK for a long time and have stronger connections here than in the country you came from. You might not be able to get evidence that you want to submit, or you might be frustrated by some of the reasons why your case was refused. Understanding a refusal is important for knowing why you were refused and what information or evidence could be useful. Understanding the law can help you know how the Home Office will look at a new case and what information or evidence you need to provide. Many people in this situation may feel that they have no real choice but to stay in the UK, even if they have been told to leave. They may know that they could have no money or housing and they may not be able to work or get support.  Often people rely on their friends, family or their communities for support with a place to sleep, food, phone credit, toiletries, clothing and other everyday things we all need to live safely and with dignity while they think about their next steps. The reality is that many people will also choose to work, or depend on arrangements in exchange for money, food, accommodation and other things they need to survive. For some people, this can look and feel like community support and collective safety. For others, it can involve pressure,  unfair treatment or unsafe situations. Understanding the risks you may face can help you make informed choices and think about how to keep yourself safe. This includes risks linked to living in the UK without leave to remain, or doing something that your immigration status does not allow. These situations are often created by immigration rules that restrict people’s access to work, housing and support, so the choices available to you may already be very limited.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you have nowhere to live, you might be able to find a homelessness shelter in your local area.Shelters are usually temporary.This means that you might be told that you can only stay in the shelter at night, or for a short amount of time, and you usually can’t leave any belongings there. Sometimes, a shelter will say that they cannot help you because of your immigration status. This is usually because they can’t access any money to pay for people who have NRPF to stay in the shelter. If the weather is extreme (usually when it is very cold), the local government can issue a ‘severe weather provision’. This means that they can give you a place to stay while this is happening, even if you have NRPF, because the weather means it could be dangerous to sleep outside. If the weather is very cold, or there is a big storm, you can try to go to a local shelter and ask if there are any special provisions in place.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: If you are in the UK on a work visa, your permission to stay may be linked to an employer that has agreed to sponsor you.This usually means the employer has been approved by the Home Office to employ migrant workers and has given you a Certificate of Sponsorship for your visa application. Whilst many sponsors are genuine, there are some recruitment agencies that exploit migrant workers. This can include asking you to repay visa fees or sponsorship fees, or failing to give you enough hours or pay you as agreed. Sometimes employers will threaten to cancel your sponsorship if you complain or refuse to do what they tell you. If you are worried about your sponsor or employer, this does not necessarily mean that you have no options. Depending on your situation, you may be able to find a new sponsor, make a different application to stay in the UK, or get advice about other steps you can take.Read more about thishere.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Paragraph Text: Destitution means being in a situation where you cannot afford your basic needs like food, shelter, warmth and water.You might be facing destitution if you do not have enough money to pay your rent, to pay for food, to pay your bills, or to heat your home, or if you have nowhere to live. The word ‘destitute’ is sometimes used to describe a person who is experiencing destitution. On this page, we refer to ‘people experiencing destitution’ and ‘people who are made destitute’. Destitution can happen to anybody, and it can happen for many different reasons.If you have migrated to the UK, many of these reasons could relate to your immigration status. This is because different types of immigration status have different conditions which affect which support and services you can access. These restrictions  mean that migrant communities are at higher risk of being made destitute. Circumstances that might mean you are at a higher risk of destitution might include: • If you are not allowed to work in the UK • If you have been asked to leave your accommodation • If your income is not enough to cover your living costs • If there is a change in your circumstances e.g. you lose your job, or have a baby • If you are responsible for other people (for their living costs or their care) • If you have experienced exploitation or abuse

Source Name: Right to Remain - Destitution and Housing
Section Heading: What support can I get if I need somewhere to stay, or have no money?
Paragraph Text: If you are experiencing destitution, there are different types of support that you might be able to access.Some types of support are only given to people with a certain immigration status, and others depend on your circumstances including: • Your income and living costs • If you are responsible for a child • If you are caring for someone • If you have a medical condition that affects your ability to look after yourself • If you have a disability and need special equipment or care • If you have a mental health condition and have been kept in hospital because of this To understand which types of support you might qualify for, you will need to check and confirm your immigration status.If you are not sure about this, then you can ask for a copy of your home office records by making a subject access request.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Paragraph Text: On this page, you will find the following information: • What happens when the Home Office grants status?Refugee StatusWhat happens after you get refugee status?Humanitarian ProtectionOther leave to remainDiscretionary LeaveApplying for British Citizenship • What happens after you get refugee status? • Humanitarian Protection • Other leave to remainDiscretionary Leave • Discretionary Leave • Applying for British Citizenship • What happens after a Home Office refusal?Resources about refusals in other languages (Amharic, Arabic, Farsi, French, Oromo, Pashto, Sorani, Tigrinya)YouTube video on refusals • Resources about refusals in other languages (Amharic, Arabic, Farsi, French, Oromo, Pashto, Sorani, Tigrinya) • YouTube video on refusals • Do you have a right appeal?What if I don’t have a right appeal? • What if I don’t have a right appeal? • If you already have a legal aid lawyerIf your legal aid lawyer says they cannot continue to help you for your appeal • If your legal aid lawyer says they cannot continue to help you for your appeal • If you get asylum support (money and/or housing from the Home Office) • Actions you can take after being refused by the Home Office If the Home Office accepts your story and evidence and agrees that you need protection in the UK – they make a positive decision on your asylum claim – you will be granted leave to remain in the UK. You may hear this described as getting “immigration status”, “permission to stay in the UK”, or getting “papers”. You may be granted Refugee Status or Humanitarian Protection, or sometimes another form of leave to remain.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Paragraph Text: • Think about what might happen next, and make a plan of action.After a refusal, you need to think about what your options are and what might come next. If your asylum or human rights claim has been refused, use the diagram above to see what the process involves after this point.Read the section on appeal rights, above. Prepare yourself for the appeal if you have the right to appeal the decision. If you don’t have the right to appeal the decision, read our pages onjudicial reviews andfresh claims.If your lawyer says they can no longer work on your case, you can look for a new lawyer and think about how to explain your case is strong. Read more on ourinformation about lawyers page.If there are weaknesses in your case (where the Home Office say they do not believe you) can you get evidence to support your story? Read the Evidence sections above. You could use this to convince a new lawyer to take on your case, or to appeal the refusal if you have to continue without a lawyer. • Stay strong, and look after yourself.Going through the asylum system is very difficult and stressful. Sometimes it can be hard to think about anything else. But constant worry about your case can leave you feeling emotionally exhausted, and less able to cope with the process.Everyone has a different way of coping – think about what works for you. While your immigration status is of course very important, it’s also important to try and give yourself a break from thinking about it. Think about activities that can distract you or help you relax for at least a short period every day, which can help your mind and body recover a little.Talk to people you trust. You may be very upset or even feel ashamed if your application/claim is refused, but don’t hide it from people. You’re going to need people to help you – don’t be afraid to ask for their solidarity.Don’t leave it till it’s too late for them to do anything. • You may wish tospeak to your MPabout your refusal, especially if you don’t have the right to appeal. Think about how to explain what has happened clearly and calmly. What has gone wrong? Why is the decision unjust? What do you want your MP to do about it? Read morehere.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Paragraph Text: If you do not have a right of appeal, your letter may say you can ask for anadministrative review. This is asking the Home Office to check whether they made a caseworking error. It can take 12 months or more to get the result.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Paragraph Text: Discretionary Leave (DL) is a type of temporary immigration status which is granted by the Home Office in ‘limited circumstances’. You cannot apply for Discretionary Leave from abroad, and it cannot be granted if you qualify for refugee status or humanitarian protection (HP) or for family or private life reasons. According to the Home Officeguidance, “where Discretionary Leave (DL) is granted, the duration of leave must be determined by considering the individual facts of the case but leave should not normally be granted for more than 30 months (2 and a half years) at a time. When an individual is granted an initial period of DL, this does not necessarily mean they will be entitled to further leave or to settlement. Subsequent periods of leave may be granted providing the applicant continues to meet the relevant criteria set out in the published policy on DL applicable at the time of the decision”. In somemodern slavery/traffickingcases, Discretionary Leave may be granted. This may be if asylum is refused or was not sought, but there are particular circumstances meaning that you, as a recognised victim of trafficking need to stay in the UK. This includes situations where you are assisting the police with inquiries, or where there are particularly compelling personal circumstances. Read more about the National Referral Mechanism and modern slavery in our Key Guidehere. Some medical cases may also result in Discretionary Leave, if removal would breach your Article 3 (right to protection from torture or degrading treatment) or Article 8 (right to private and family life) rights under theEuropean Convention on Human Rights(ECHR). If you have Discretionary Leave, you can apply forsettlementafter: • 6 years if you were first given Discretionary Leave on or before 8 July 2012 • 10 years if you were first given Discretionary Leave from 9 July 2012 • You must still meet the eligibility criteria for your type of leave. Check your documents to see what your criteria are If you have Discretionary Leave it costs£2,885 for you and each other person you includein your application for settlement. You’ll each need to have your biometric information (fingerprints and a photo) taken, too. You should apply for settlement during thelast month of your current permissionto be in the UK. You must apply online. Learn more about the application process and the form you will need to fill outhere. If your application for indefinite leave to remain isrefused, you might still be able to stay in the UK. Your decision letter will explain what you’ve been offered instead of indefinite leave to remain. In rare circumstances, another kind of leave calledRestricted Leavemay be granted. For example, if you are excluded from receiving Refugee Status or Humanitarian Protection, but your Article 3 rights under the ECHR would be breached if you were removed from the UK. Applying for permanent residence (Citizenship) in the UK If you are granted refugee status or humanitarian protection, you can apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) in the UK after spending 5 years in the UK. ILR is sometimes called ‘settled status’. You can learn more about applying for ILRhere. After having ILR for 12 months, and if you meet the ‘good character’ requirements, you can apply for British citizenship. This is sometimes called ‘naturalisation’. You can learn more about applying for British citizenshiphere. If you have humanitarian protection, you will typically be granted5 years’leave to remain in the UK. At the end of this period, you will be eligible to apply for ILR (settled status) in the UK. After having ILR for 12 months, you will be able to apply for British citizenship. Important:If you are granted humanitarian protection after claiming asylumon or after 2 March 2026,you will now usually be given 30 months (2.5 years) permission to stay on the protection route. If your claim was made on or before 1 March 2026, the Rules keep the minimum 5 years grant for refugee status and humanitarian protection. What happens after a Home Office refusal? A Home Office refusal can feel shocking and upsetting. But it does not always mean your case is over.Some people can make a legal challenge. This is called anappeal(a judge looks at the Home Office decision).Read more about appealshere. If you have alawyeror legal adviser, contact themas soon as possible. If you do not have one, you can still take steps to protect your case.First, read your decision letter. You (and your lawyer, if you have one) will need to read the Home Office decision letter carefully. In asylum cases this is often called a Reasons for Refusal Letter (RFRL). It should explain whether you have aright of appeal(and the deadline), or a different review option and why the Home Office refused your case. If you are appealingin the UK, the Home Office says you usually have14 days from the date you received the decision letter. If you areoutside the UK, it is usually28 days from the date you received the decision letter. Always check what your letter says. Click on the buttons below for translated summaries of this section on refusals (or use the Google Translate tool in the top left hand corner): Video in other languages:

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Section Heading: Do you have a right of appeal?
Paragraph Text: Not all Home Office decisions come with a right of appeal. Your Home Office decision letter should tell you whether you have an appeal right. You can appeal a decision if the Home Office has: • refused your protection claim (also known as ‘asylum claim’ or ‘humanitarian protection’) • refused your human rights claim (this includes claims raising health, family and private life grounds) • revoked (this means taken away) your protection status • revoked your British citizenship • refused you a residence document or deported you under the Immigration (European Economic Area) Regulations 2016 • refused or revoked your status, varied (changed) the length or condition of your stay, or deported you under the EU Settlement Scheme • refused or revoked your travel permit or family permit under the EU Settlement Scheme or restricted your rights to enter or leave the UK under those permits • refused or revoked your permit, or deported you if you’re afrontier worker • refused or revoked your leave, or deported you if you’re anS2 healthcare visitor Some asylum or human rights claims are “certified” by the Home Office. This means the Home Office is saying your claim is clearly not true or clearly cannot succeed (they may use the words “clearly unfounded”). If your claim is certified (sometimes the letter may mention “section 94”), you usually cannot appeal from inside the UK. This does not always mean there is nothing you can do but you may need urgent legal advice about other options, for example a judicial review (a court challenge about whether the Home Office made the decision not to give you a right of appeal lawfully and fairly). If you have a lawyer and they think the Home Office decision is very bad and major errors have been made, they may contact the Home Office before making submitting an appeal to ask them to reconsider their decision. This is only likely to succeed in a very strong case. If you made another type of application (that isn’t in the list above)before6 April 2015 you may still have the right of appeal if your case is refused. See the Home Office website for more informationhere. If you are making a human rights claim when you are subject to deportation after a criminal sentence, the Home Office may certify the claim unless you can show that “serious and irreversible harm” would occur if you had to appeal outside of the UK. The Home Office is less likely to certify your claim if your child is a British citizen. Read more on theDeportation pageof this guide.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Section Heading: If you already have a legal aid lawyer
Paragraph Text: If you have a legal aid lawyer (a lawyer paid for by theLegal Aid Agencybecause you cannot afford to pay), they may need to decide if they can keep representing you after a refusal. This is called amerits test.Merits test means the lawyer must check whether your appeal has a strong enough chance of success for legal aid funding. In general, legal aid usually requires the lawyer to assess that the case has at least a 50% chance of success (sometimes called “moderate” prospects). There are some exceptions in certain situations. This is a requirement of the Legal Aid Agency, not the lawyer’s personal choice. If you have a private lawyer (you pay fees), you will usually need to pay for the appeal work. They should still be honest with you about whether they think your appeal is strong enough to succeed, and explain their reasons. If your legal aid lawyer says they cannot continue to help you for your appeal: • ask them to explain the reasons clearly. If they tell you they are completing aCW4 formthen please readthis page. • ask what options you have next (for example, getting a second opinion) • Remember thedeadlinein your refusal letter. If your lawyer is closing your case, you can ask them to lodge (submit) your appeal onlinebeforethey close your file to help protect the deadline. If they agree to lodge it, ask them to confirm in writing that the appeal has been submitted, and to send you the date and time it was submitted, your Tribunal/HMCTS reference number (if available), and a copy of what they submitted. If you change lawyers, the new lawyer will usually need your HMCTS reference number to take over the appeal. • If they don’t agree then you can do it yourself online (or with the help of a trusted person) and keep looking for advice. If you get asylum support (money and/or housing from the Home Office) If you are getting asylum support, it should usually continue while your appeal is ongoing, as long as you lodge (submit) your appeal in time. That is why it is so important not to miss the appeal deadline in your refusal letter. It is also important to make sure the Home Office and your lawyer have your correct contact details, especially your email address and phone number, so you do not miss important messages about your decision, deadlines, or support.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Section Heading: Judicial review (court challenge about how the decision was made)
Paragraph Text: A judicial review is not the same as an appeal. An appeal is about the substance of your case. A judicial review is usually about whether the Home Office made the decision lawfully and fairly (the process). For example: did the Home Office follow the correct rules and take relevant evidence into account. A judicial review can also be used to challenge the Home Office decision torefuse you a right of appeal. Judicial review is complicated and has time limits. If you can, get legal advice as soon as possible. Read more on theJudicial Reviews page of this guide. If you have a right of appeal, the next step is to lodge your appeal in time. See ourPreparing your appeal pagefor what to do on the day you receive a refusal and the step-by-step process.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Home Office Decision
Section Heading: What happens when the Home Office grants status after an asylum application?
Paragraph Text: A grant of refugee status If the Home Office decides that you have a need for protection because you are at risk of persecution, and your claim falls under the grounds for protection in the Refugee Convention, you will be granted Refugee Status for a period of 5 years. After this time, you can apply forsettlement(also known as ‘indefinite leave to remain’) in the UK. After 1 year of settlement, you will be able to apply for British citizenship (a British passport).  You can read more about this in the ‘Applying for British Citizenship’section of this pagebelow.There are changes coming this year but as of March 2026, the 5 year route to settlement for protection routes remains in place. If you are granted refugee status after claiming asylumon or after 2 March 2026,you will usually be given 30 months (2.5 years) permission to stay on the protection route. If your asylum claim wasmade on or before 1 March 2026,the Rules keep the minimum 5 years grant for refugee status and humanitarian protection. • Someone claims asylum on 20 February 2026, but gets a decision granting refugee status (or Humanitarian Protection) on 10 June 2026 – they should be granted at least 5 years’ leave to remain because theirclaim dateisbefore2 March. • Someone claims asylum on 2 March 2026 and is granted refugee status (or Humanitarian Protection) on 10 June 2026 under the new rules they should be granted 30 months’ leave. The rules saythat unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC) will still be given 5 years leave to remain.This means that if you were under 18 when you claimed asylum and you were alone (without a parent or legal guardian), you should still be given 5 years, not 30 months. This also applies if you turned 18 while waiting, but you would have been classed as a UASC if the decision had been made earlier. If you need to extend your permission to stay (“further permission to stay”), the rules say you should applywithin the last 28 daysbefore your leave is due to end. What happens after you receive refugee status? We know that although a grant of refugee status can be a big relief, it can also be a very overwhelming experience as many changes happen very quickly. We have a detailed Toolkit page which outlines what happens after you receive refugee status (including information on housing, family reunion, getting a bank account, receiving benefits, and more). A grant of humanitarian protection Refugee status (see above) should be granted if you can show you are at risk of specific,individualpersecution. If you are fleeing war or violence that is threatening or harmingmany peoplewhere you are from – not you specifically because of who you are – you maynotqualify for refugee status. If you are not at risk of individual persecution but you would be at risk of serious threat or harm if you returned to where you are from because of general violence (for example during a war or internal conflict), then you may be granted another form of immigration status calledHumanitarian Protection. This is often referred to as ‘protection status’. Paragraphs339C-CA of the Immigration Rulesset out the basis on which a person will be granted humanitarian protection: 339C. An asylum applicant will be granted humanitarian protection in the United Kingdom if the Secretary of State is satisfied that: (i) they are in the United Kingdom or have arrived at a port of entry in the United Kingdom; (ii) they are not a refugee within the meaning of Article 1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention; (iii) substantial grounds have been shown for believing that the person concerned, if returned to the country of origin would face a real risk of serious harm and is unable, or, owing to such risk, unwilling to avail themselves of the protection of that country; and (iv) they are not excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection. Serious harmincludes the death penalty, unlawful killing, torture or punishment in the country of origin, or a threat to life due to indiscriminate violence or armed conflict. If you qualify for refugee status, you willnotbe granted humanitarian protection, even if you specifically apply for it (paragraph 334of the Immigration Rules). People who receive humanitarian protection status are granted leave to remain for 5 years, and enjoy almost all of the same rights as those with refugee status.Important:If you are granted humanitarian protection after claiming asylumon or after 2 March 2026,you will now usually be given 30 months (2.5 years) permission to stay on the protection route. If your claim was made on or before 1 March 2026, the Rules keep the minimum 5 years grant for refugee status and humanitarian protection. If you are granted Humanitarian Protection and you would like totravel, you will either need to use your national passport or if you can show that you cannot do this, you canapply for a Certificate of Travelfrom the Home Office. If you receive a grant of Humanitarian Protection, you may apply forsettlement(indefinite leave to remain) in the UK if you fulfil the following requirements: • You have a residence card showing that you have humanitarian protection,and • You have had humanitarian protection status in the UK for 5 years. There isnoapplication fee for you to apply for settlement with Humanitarian Protection, and this will also apply to your partner or child. You should apply during thelast monthof your current permission to be in the UK. You must apply online. You can learn more about the application process and the form you will need to fill outhere. If your application for settlement isrefused, you might still be able to stay in the UK. Your decision letter from the Home Office will explain what you’ve been offered instead of indefinite leave to remain. Other leave to remain In some cases, your asylum claim may be refused but you may be granted another type of leave to remain in the UK. If you have applied for asylum, and that application is refused, you may be granted leave under the immigration rules (on human rights grounds, for example). You can read more about thishere. If you are anunaccompanied minorand there are not adequate reception arrangements in your country of origin, the Home Office may grant you limited leave to remain until you are 17.5 years old.

Paragraph Text: The Right to Remain Toolkit is free to use, and it’s for people who want to learn more about the legal process, or a particular part of the legal process. You might be making an application or are thinking about it; you might be helping someone else to do so.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Toolkit Home
Paragraph Text: The information in this guide comes from experts – from people who are going through the legal process or have done in the past, from those helping them, from lawyers, from community groups. It covers different stages of the legal system and procedures, with detailed information on rights and options at each stage, and suggestions about actions you can take to be in a better situation, or to help someone else. Read more about this guide on theAbout page. Find the information you need for your situation using the contents bar on each page – there’s information about asylum cases, human rights cases, and immigration cases. Your situation might fall into more than one of these categories.

Source Name: Right to Remain - Toolkit Home
Paragraph Text: Understanding the asylum and immigration system, and your own legal case, is very important. Many people have to make their way through this very complicated system without legal representation (without a lawyer). Even if you have a lawyer, it’s important to understand your own legal case – this is your case and your life and you need to keep track of what is happening and whether the lawyer is doing the things they should be.
